intro: The best heat pump water heater for most homes in 2026 is the Rheem ProTerra 50-gallon hybrid, which Rheem rates at a UEF from the high 3s to about 4, meaning it turns each unit of electricity into three to four units of heat. Bigger families, homes with a full electrical panel and cold-climate houses each have a better match below.

A heat pump water heater works like a refrigerator in reverse, pulling warmth out of the surrounding air and pushing it into the tank. That is why it uses so little electricity, and also why it has rules a regular tank does not: it needs breathing room, it works best in a space that stays above the 40s, and it reheats more slowly than the heater you have now.
quickAnswer: Buy the Rheem ProTerra Hybrid 50-gallon if you have a basement or garage with room around it and a 240-volt circuit. Four or more people should step up to the 66-gallon A.O. Smith Voltex AL, homes where a new circuit would mean a panel upgrade should choose the Rheem ProTerra Plug-In 120V in a larger size, and cold-climate homes with no good indoor spot should look at the SanCO2 split system.

blocks.p: Three things decide which one fits: air space around the tank, the electrical circuit available and how much hot water your busiest hour uses. Get those right and almost any of these units will cut the electricity used for hot water by well over half compared with a resistance tank.
Buy one size larger than the tank you are replacing. If gas is still on the table, compare these with our [best gas water heater](/best-gas-water-heater/) picks before you decide.

sections.h: The 6 Best Heat Pump Water Heaters in 2026, Ranked

blocks.p: Each of these six is matched to a type of house rather than ranked on a single efficiency number, because a heat pump water heater that tops the charts still disappoints if it is too small for the family, too tall for the basement or parked in a freezing garage. The order weighs published UEF and first hour ratings, operating temperature range, air-space needs, warranty terms, installation demands and what owners and installers report over time.

The ProTerra is Rheem's flagship hybrid, and the 50-gallon version is where most households should start. Rheem lists a Uniform Energy Factor from the high 3s to around 4 depending on the exact version, among the highest ratings sold, so it uses a fraction of the electricity of a resistance tank. Several modes let you lean toward maximum savings or faster recovery, and connected versions add an app for scheduling, vacation mode, energy tracking and leak alerts, which earns its keep on a 50-gallon tank sitting in a finished basement. Rheem covers the tank and parts for up to 10 years. Site needs are typical for an integrated hybrid: a 240-volt circuit, a condensate drain and several hundred cubic feet of surrounding air, or louvered doors or ducting in a smaller room. Owners commonly report a large drop in the water-heating part of their electric bill, with the expected note that recovery is slower in heat-pump-only mode.
**Pros:** UEF in the high 3s to about 4 by version; multiple operating modes; app with leak detection on connected versions; up to 10-year warranty per Rheem.
**Cons:** Needs a 240-volt circuit and a condensate drain; needs plenty of surrounding air.
[Check price on Amazon](https://www.amazon.com/s?k=Rheem+ProTerra+hybrid+heat+pump+water+heater+50+gallon&tag=sktiger-20)

blocks.h3: Best for Big Households: A.O. Smith Voltex AL Hybrid 66-Gallon

blocks.p: The most common complaint about heat pump water heaters is running out of hot water, and the usual cause is buying the same size as the old electric tank. A heat pump reheats more slowly, so a bigger tank fixes it, and A.O. Smith builds the Voltex AL in sizes up to 80 gallons. The 66-gallon model fits a household of four or five, with hybrid-mode first hour delivery that keeps pace with a run of morning showers. Efficiency ratings stay strong across the line, so stepping up in size adds little to the running cost. Current versions add connected controls for scheduling and monitoring. The compromises are bulk and price. A 66-gallon unit is tall, wide and heavy, and the heat pump module on top adds height, so measure ceiling clearance, stairwells and doorways before ordering. It costs more than a 50-gallon unit, but for a bigger household that premium is cheaper than a decade of short showers.
**Pros:** Sizes up to 80 gallons; strong hybrid-mode first hour delivery; good efficiency across the line; widely supported by installers.
**Cons:** Large and heavy; costs more than 50-gallon units.
[Check price on Amazon](https://www.amazon.com/s?k=A.O.+Smith+Voltex+AL+hybrid+heat+pump+water+heater+66+gallon&tag=sktiger-20)

The cost that surprises people switching from gas is usually electrical. A standard hybrid needs its own 240-volt, typically 30-amp circuit, and in a full panel that work can approach the price of the heater. Rheem's ProTerra Plug-In runs on an ordinary 120-volt outlet, and certain configurations are designed to share an existing circuit, which can turn a panel upgrade into a plug-in job. That makes it the most practical answer to the 120-volt heat pump water heater searches that keep growing. What you give up is recovery. A 120-volt unit relies mostly on its heat pump, without the large resistance elements a 240-volt hybrid uses to catch up, so it reheats more slowly after heavy use. Rheem sells it in 50- and 65-gallon sizes to compensate, and the larger tank is the right call for anything beyond a small household. Owners who sized up commonly say they never notice; owners who did not often run short.
**Pros:** Plugs into a standard 120-volt outlet; some versions share an existing circuit; high efficiency rating; larger tank sizes available.
**Cons:** Slower recovery than 240-volt hybrids; little or no resistance backup, so sizing up is essential.
[Check price on Amazon](https://www.amazon.com/s?k=Rheem+ProTerra+plug-in+120V+heat+pump+water+heater&tag=sktiger-20)

blocks.h3: Best Plumber-Installed: Bradford White AeroTherm Series

blocks.p: Bradford White sells only through professional plumbers, and its AeroTherm series is built around that model: a heat pump water heater supplied, installed and supported by the contractor who fits it. The range runs from 50 to 80 gallons, so a plumber can match capacity to the household without switching brands, and several operating modes cover everything from efficiency-first to high demand. Plumbers have long rated Bradford White tanks as durable, and the AeroTherm brings that reputation to hybrids. It puts less weight on apps and connected features than Rheem, which some owners like and others miss. Because it is bought through a contractor, the price comes bundled with markup and labor, so comparing quotes takes more effort, but you get one point of contact for service and warranty claims. If a plumber you already trust carries Bradford White, this is a well-supported choice that is likely to be installed correctly the first time.
**Pros:** Plumber-supplied with a single support contact; 50- to 80-gallon range; multiple operating modes; installer reputation for durability.
**Cons:** Not sold at retail, so pricing comes through a quote; fewer smart features than some rivals.
[Check price on Amazon](https://www.amazon.com/s?k=Bradford+White+AeroTherm+heat+pump+water+heater&tag=sktiger-20)

blocks.h3: Best Value: Ruud Ultra Series Hybrid 50-Gallon

blocks.p: Ruud and Rheem share a parent company, and the Ruud Ultra Series hybrid shares much of its engineering with Rheem's heat pump water heaters. The efficiency rating sits in the same high range, the operating modes are similar, and parts and service knowledge overlap heavily, which helps over a 10- to 15-year ownership. The difference is how you buy it. Ruud sells mainly through contractors rather than home centers, so it usually shows up inside an installation quote, and contractors who carry it often price it below a ProTerra of the same size. Connected features vary by version, so if leak alerts or app control matter to you, confirm the exact model number before signing. Owners and installers generally describe it as efficient and dependable, with little separating it from its Rheem sibling beyond the badge. If one of your quotes comes back with a Ruud hybrid at a lower number, there is little reason to hold out for the Rheem.
**Pros:** Shares engineering with Rheem hybrids; high efficiency rating; multiple modes; often quoted below the ProTerra.
**Cons:** Mostly sold through installers; connected features vary by version.
[Check price on Amazon](https://www.amazon.com/s?k=Ruud+Ultra+Series+hybrid+heat+pump+water+heater+50+gallon&tag=sktiger-20)

blocks.h3: Best for Cold Climates: SanCO2 Split Heat Pump Water Heater

blocks.p: The SanCO2 moves the heat pump outdoors. A compact outdoor unit using carbon dioxide as its refrigerant heats the water and sends it through insulated lines to a separate storage tank inside. That layout removes two weaknesses of integrated hybrids. The indoor tank does not cool or dry the room and makes no compressor noise in the house. And the maker rates the CO2 heat pump to keep running at outdoor temperatures well below freezing, while integrated units need surrounding air that stays above roughly the low 40s. CO2 systems also make very hot water efficiently, so with a mixing valve a smaller tank supplies more usable hot water. The drawbacks are cost and installation. The system typically costs several times as much as an integrated hybrid, and it needs an installer familiar with split systems plus a place outside for the unit. For a tight, well-insulated home in a cold region, or a house with no good indoor spot, it is the strongest option.
**Pros:** Outdoor CO2 heat pump rated for well below freezing per the maker; no indoor noise or room cooling; very hot output; works where indoor air space is limited.
**Cons:** Several times the cost of an integrated hybrid; needs a specialist installer and an outdoor location.

sections.h: How Does a Heat Pump Water Heater Work?

blocks.p: It moves heat instead of making it. A fan draws room air across an evaporator coil, a compressor raises the temperature of the heat it collects, and a condenser passes that heat into the water. Cooler, drier air blows out the other side.

A resistance element turns electricity directly into heat, so its efficiency tops out near 100 percent, which is why resistance tanks carry a UEF of about 0.9. A heat pump spends electricity moving heat that is already in the air, so it delivers several times more heat than the power it draws. The best units carry UEFs of roughly 3.5 to 4.

Most residential models also have resistance elements that switch on when demand outruns the heat pump or the air gets too cold. The operating mode decides how readily those elements kick in, and the elements are where most of the savings leak away.

blocks.h3: What is the latest heat pump water heater technology?

blocks.p: Three developments stand out. Plug-in 120-volt models remove the need for a new 240-volt circuit. Split systems using CO2 refrigerant put the compressor outdoors and keep working in deep cold. And connected controls let a unit shift heating to off-peak hours on time-of-use rates. Federal rules are pushing the market the same way: the Department of Energy finalized standards in 2024 that, from 2029, effectively require heat pump technology for most new electric storage water heaters in common sizes.

blocks.h3: Using one with hard water or radiant heat

blocks.p: Hard water builds scale on any tank, so plan on draining sediment yearly and consider a softener; our [home water filtration guide](/best-water-filtration-system-for-home/) explains what treats hardness and what does not. Some owners also ask about radiant floor heating. A standard integrated unit is sized for domestic hot water, so pairing one with a radiant system is a design question for a heating contractor rather than a plug-and-play upgrade.

sections.h: Should You Buy a 240V, 120V or Split Heat Pump Water Heater?

blocks.p: Choose a 240-volt hybrid when the circuit exists or is cheap to add, a 120-volt plug-in when the panel is full, and a split system only for cold climates or homes with no suitable indoor space.

The most common and most flexible type. It needs a dedicated 240-volt circuit, typically 30 amps, and recovers quickly in hybrid mode thanks to its resistance elements. When it replaces an electric resistance tank, the circuit is usually already there.

Built for homes where a new 240-volt circuit would be costly. It plugs into a standard outlet, and some versions can share a circuit. It leans almost entirely on the heat pump, so recovery is slower and a larger tank is what makes it livable. It is especially useful when replacing a gas tank.

The heat pump sits outside and the tank inside, linked by lines. It handles cold climates better, makes no noise indoors and does not cool the room. It costs far more and needs a specialist installer.

sections.h: What Size Heat Pump Water Heater Do You Need?

blocks.p: One step larger than the tank you are replacing. In heat-pump-only mode a heat pump recovers more slowly than a resistance tank and much more slowly than gas, so a household happy with a 40-gallon electric tank usually does better with a 50 or 65, and one that used a 50 is a strong candidate for a 65 or 66.

Compare models by the first hour rating on the EnergyGuide label. Add up your busiest hour: about 10 to 20 gallons per shower, about 6 for the dishwasher and more for warm laundry. The rating should clear that total comfortably in the mode you plan to run.

blocks.h3: A bigger tank does not waste energy

blocks.p: A larger tank gives the heat pump more time to work before the resistance elements are needed, which saves more than the slightly higher standby loss costs. On a well-insulated modern tank, the bigger size usually lowers the bill.
A heat pump water heater is a 10- to 15-year purchase. If teenagers are on the way or guests stay often, size for that household now.

sections.h: Where Can You Install a Heat Pump Water Heater?

blocks.p: In a space with several hundred cubic feet of air, enough height for a taller unit and a drain nearby, which usually means a basement or garage rather than a closet.

Makers generally ask for several hundred cubic feet around the unit, often 450 to 1,000 depending on the model, or a smaller room with louvered doors or ducting. A typical basement or garage clears that easily.
The heat pump module sits on top, so these tanks are often six feet tall or more. Measure to the lowest duct, pipe or joist and add the service clearance the manual lists for the filter.

The heat pump pulls moisture from the air and drips a steady stream of water whenever it runs. It needs a drain line to a floor drain, sink or condensate pump. Make sure the installation quote says where that line goes.

The unit cools and dries the space. In a damp summer basement that is a bonus and can lighten the load on a [basement dehumidifier](/best-dehumidifier-for-basement/), though it does not replace real moisture control. In a space shared with living areas in winter, the cooling adds a little to the heating load.
Skip spaces next to a clothes dryer, where lint clogs the air filter, and closets beside bedrooms, where the hum can grate.

sections.h: Will a Heat Pump Water Heater Work in a Cold Garage?

blocks.p: Only partly. Colder air holds less heat to collect, so efficiency drops as the space cools. Below a cutoff, typically around 37 to 45 degrees depending on the model, an integrated unit switches entirely to its resistance elements and acts like an ordinary electric tank.

A basement that holds in the 50s and 60s all year is close to ideal. An attached garage in a mild climate also works well. A detached or uninsulated garage in a cold climate can force resistance mode for months each winter and erase much of the yearly savings.

Ducting the intake and exhaust to warmer spaces can help, and insulating and air-sealing the garage raises its winter temperature. In a truly cold climate with no good indoor spot, a split system like the SanCO2 avoids the problem by keeping the heat pump outside.
Leave a min-max thermometer in the planned spot through a cold snap. If it rarely drops below the high 40s, an integrated hybrid will deliver most of its rated savings.

sections.h: How Much Does a Heat Pump Water Heater Save and Cost?

blocks.p: Against an electric resistance tank, commonly 60 to 75 percent of the water-heating bill. For a family of four that is often a few hundred dollars a year, depending on use and electricity price. Each model's EnergyGuide label shows an estimated yearly cost at national average prices, which is the easiest way to compare two units.

Replacing a resistance tank where the 240-volt circuit already exists, the extra cost of a heat pump model often comes back in roughly three to six years. Against gas the math is weaker, because gas is cheaper per unit of heat in many areas and the switch may need new electrical work. Where gas is cheap, payback can stretch out or never arrive.

Installers commonly quote roughly $3,000 to $5,000 including the unit to swap an electric resistance tank for a 240-volt hybrid. A gas-to-heat-pump conversion that needs a new circuit runs higher, a 120-volt plug-in can shrink the electrical portion, and split systems cost significantly more. Many jurisdictions require permits for both the plumbing and the electrical work.

The federal 25C tax credit, which covered 30 percent of a qualifying heat pump water heater up to $2,000, was ended by 2025 federal legislation for equipment placed in service after December 31, 2025. State programs and utility rebates may still apply depending on where you live, so check eligibility rules before you buy, and confirm tax questions with a professional.
A failed tank forces a rushed decision, and the installer may only carry conventional tanks. Collecting quotes and confirming electrical capacity ahead of time lets you switch on your own schedule.

sections.h: Which Mode Should You Run, and How Loud Is It?

blocks.p: Run hybrid or energy-saver mode as the default. It captures most of the savings while calling in the resistance elements when demand spikes. If you rarely run short, try heat-pump-only mode for a few weeks; switch to high-demand mode when guests visit and back again when they leave.

Heat-pump-only mode runs the compressor alone for the lowest cost and slowest recovery. Hybrid mode leans on the heat pump and adds the elements under heavy demand. High-demand mode uses the elements freely. Electric mode runs elements only, which helps for troubleshooting or in very cold spaces.

About 120 degrees suits most homes and lowers scald risk. Some households set it higher with a thermostatic mixing valve to stretch usable hot water. Vacation mode lowers the setpoint while you are away, and connected models can schedule it from an app.
Published sound levels are typically in the mid-40s to mid-50s decibels, often compared to a refrigerator or a window air conditioner on low. Most owners stop noticing it in a basement or garage.

Expected life is commonly 10 to 15 years. Clean the air filter every few months, keep the condensate line clear, drain a few gallons from the tank once a year, test the relief valve and check the anode rod every few years where the design has one. Outside warranty, a failed compressor can make replacement the better deal on an older unit.

mistakes: Buying the same size as the old tank

A heat pump reheats more slowly than the electric or gas tank it replaces, especially in efficiency mode. Matching the old 40 or 50 gallons is the top reason owners run out of hot water. Go up one size and compare models by first hour rating, not gallons.
Squeezing it into a small closet

Integrated units need several hundred cubic feet of air. Shut in a tight closet without louvered doors or ducting, the unit chills the space, loses efficiency and falls back on its resistance elements. Check the air-volume requirement in the manual before choosing a spot.

Whenever the heat pump runs, it makes water. Without a drain line to a floor drain, sink or condensate pump, that water ends up on the floor, where it damages flooring and invites mold. Make sure the quote states where the drain line runs.

High-demand and electric modes rely on the resistance elements and erase much of the efficiency gain. Owners often switch during a busy week and never switch back. Keep hybrid or energy-saver mode as the default and use faster modes only when you need them.

The federal 25C credit ended for equipment placed in service after 2025, and rebate programs change often. Counting on money that no longer exists breaks the payback math. Confirm current state and utility programs and their eligibility rules before you buy.
bottomLine: For most homes with a basement or garage and a 240-volt circuit, the Rheem ProTerra 50-gallon hybrid is the heat pump water heater to buy. Move up to the 66-gallon A.O. Smith Voltex AL for four or more people, pick the Rheem ProTerra Plug-In in a larger size when the panel is full, take a Bradford White AeroTherm or Ruud Ultra when your plumber carries them, and consider the SanCO2 split for cold climates despite its price. Whatever you choose, buy one size larger than the old tank, confirm air space, power and a drain before ordering, and leave it in hybrid mode. Do those three things and it should cut the electricity you spend on hot water by well over half for a decade or more.

faqs.q: What is the best rated heat pump water heater?
faqs.a: The Rheem ProTerra 50-gallon hybrid is the best fit for most homes, with a UEF Rheem lists from the high 3s to about 4, several modes, app control on connected versions and a warranty of up to 10 years. Bigger households should step up to a 65- or 66-gallon model such as the A.O. Smith Voltex AL.

faqs.q: What is the most reliable heat pump water heater?
faqs.a: Reliability depends as much on the install as the brand. Rheem, A.O. Smith and Bradford White all have broad installer support and long warranties, and Bradford White's AeroTherm comes with a single contractor contact for service. Put the unit in a space that stays above the 40s, keep the filter and condensate drain clean, and most will reach 10 to 15 years.

faqs.q: Is there a good 120V heat pump hot water heater?
faqs.a: Yes. The Rheem ProTerra Plug-In runs on a standard 120-volt outlet, and some versions can share an existing circuit, which avoids a costly panel upgrade. It recovers more slowly than a 240-volt hybrid because it has little resistance backup, so buy the 65-gallon size for anything beyond a small household.

faqs.q: Is it worth replacing a gas water heater with a heat pump?
faqs.a: It depends on local gas and electricity prices, available rebates and whether you need new electrical work. Payback against gas is slower than against an electric resistance tank, and where gas is cheap it may never come. Many homeowners wait until the gas tank nears the end of its life, then compare installed and running costs side by side.

faqs.q: How cold can the space be for a heat pump water heater?
faqs.a: Most integrated units keep the heat pump running down to roughly 37 to 45 degrees depending on the model, then switch to resistance heat. Efficiency falls as the air cools, so spaces that stay above the high 40s give the best results. For a cold garage or cold climate, a split system with an outdoor CO2 heat pump is the better match.

faqs.q: Does a heat pump water heater work with hard water?
faqs.a: Yes, but hard water builds scale and sediment in any tank, which slows heating and shortens life. Drain a few gallons once a year, check the anode rod every few years and consider a water softener if hardness is high. A softener treats the calcium and magnesium behind scale; a carbon filter does not.

faqs.q: Do I need a new circuit for a heat pump water heater?
faqs.a: A 240-volt hybrid needs its own 240-volt circuit, typically 30 amps, which is usually in place when you replace an electric tank. Replacing a gas tank may mean running a new circuit and possibly upgrading the panel. A 120-volt plug-in model avoids that, and some can share a circuit, but they recover more slowly.
